summary: The note profiles six indigenous artists whose work in weaving, painting, pottery, cloaks, jewelry and music carries ancestral stories into the present. Each artist is tied to a specific 2023 showing or performance and to a particular nation or tradition. The note concludes that this renaissance preserves indigenous identity while giving it new forms.
one_line: Profiles of six indigenous artists in 2023 who use traditional techniques in weaving, painting, pottery, jewelry and music to carry ancestral stories forward.
key_facts: Erena Taylor, a member of the Haida nation, displayed her tapestries at the Heartbeat of Cultures Gallery on Tuesday, September 5, 2023.
Erena Taylor learned her weaving techniques from her grandmother under the cedars.
Jason Mawkibe's oil paintings draw on Métis beadwork patterns and blend them with modern abstraction; his work was shown in a gallery on October 12, 2023.
Alyssa Two-Rivers, a potter of the Pueblo people, presented her clay pieces at the Ancient Futures exhibit on November 16, 2023.
Alyssa Two-Rivers's pottery fuses earth, water, air and fire, described as the four sacred elements.
Daniel Grayhawk's traditional storytelling cloaks, made with Salish weaving techniques, took center stage on December 9, 2023.
Daniel Grayhawk's cloaks carry the stories of the Great Pacific Northwest.
Sofia White Dove, a jewelry maker from the Navajo Nation, unveiled her silver and turquoise jewelry on September 23, 2023.
Jonathan Running Wolf, a musician, performed on November 25, 2023, playing flutes handcrafted from cedar and birch.
The note concludes that the renaissance of indigenous artistry is a bridge to the past and a pathway to the future, preserving indigenous identity.
